Grokking Group Multiplication with Cosets

Dashiell Stander Affiliation: EleutherAI Correspondence to: dash.stander@gmail.com    Qinan Yu Affiliation: EleutherAI Affiliation: Brown University    Honglu Fan Affiliation: EleutherAI Affiliation: University of Geneva    Stella Biderman Affiliation: EleutherAI
Abstract

The complex and unpredictable nature of deep neural networks prevents their safe use in many high-stakes applications. There have been many techniques developed to interpret deep neural networks, but all have substantial limitations. Algorithmic tasks have proven to be a fruitful test ground for interpreting a neural network end-to-end. Building on previous work, we completely reverse engineer fully connected one-hidden layer networks that have “grokked” the arithmetic of the permutation groups S5S_{5} and S6S_{6}. The models discover the true subgroup structure of the full group and converge on neural circuits that decompose the group arithmetic using the permutation group’s subgroups. We relate how we reverse engineered the model’s mechanisms and confirmed our theory was a faithful description of the circuit’s functionality. We also draw attention to current challenges in conducting interpretability research by comparing our work to Chughtai et al. 2023 which alleges to find a different algorithm for this same problem.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, Grokking, Interpretability, Group Theory, Harmonic Analysis

1 Introduction

Many methods have been proposed to render deep neural networks interpretable. There is both an academic interest in understanding how neural networks do what they do and a societal interest in ensuring that decisions made by such models are sound, unbiased, and subject to human review. These concerns are not new, nor are they unique to deep neural networks. Many of the techniques developed (such as SHAP values [Lundberg & Lee 2017], saliency maps [Simonyan et al. 2014], gradient attribution [Shrikumar et al. 2017], dimension reduction [Wold et al. 1987], etc…) are still widely used today, but there is an understanding that such methods must be used as just one part of a careful analysis. Naive applications of even the most sophisticated algorithms will give misleading results [Adebayo et al. 2020, Bolukbasi et al. 2021, Doshi-Velez & Kim 2017, Jain & Wallace 2019].

Mechanistic interpretability seeks to find “neural circuits” within deep neural networks, small sub-networks that act as connected computation graphs and accomplish a task. In “toy” (highly constrained) settings mechanistic interpretability has been successful, with multiple examples where the inner workings of neural networks have been successfully reverse engineered end-to-end [Gromov 2023, Nanda et al. 2023a, Nanda et al. 2023b, Quirke & Barez 2024, Zhang et al. 2023]. There have also been encouraging early successes in finding interpretable circuits within real-world models [Geva et al. 2021, Lieberum et al. 2023, McGrath et al. 2023, Olsson et al. 2022, Wang et al. 2022a], but there is already work emerging that illustrates how neural networks can resist common “mechanistic interpretability” methods [Friedman et al. 2023, Makelov et al. 2023, Wen et al. 2023].

The toy interpretability projects that have succeeded have done so in large part because a distinct ground truth circuit that encodes the true nature of the task or environment emerged in the model. We build on this tradition and study a model that has perfectly learned to multiply permutations of five and six elements, which in mathematics is known as the symmetric groups S5S_{5} and S6S_{6}, which are deeply studied and well-understood objects [Diaconis 1988, Dummit & Foote 2003, Fulton & Harris, Joe 1991]. We succeed in completely reverse engineering the model and enumerating the diverse circuits that it converges on to implement the multiplication of the symmetric group. Our work does not, however, represent an unmitigated success for the project of mechanistic interpretability. The prior work of Chughtai et al. 2023 studied the exact same model and setting, but came to completely different conclusions. Understanding why our and Chughtai et al. 2023’s interpretations of the same data diverged required extensive effort (see Appendix 7 for a thorough comparison). We find that even in a setting as simple and well understood as group arithmetic, it is incredibly difficult to do interpretability research and be confident about one’s conclusions.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We completely reverse engineer a one-hidden layer fully-connected network trained on the permutation groups S5S_{5} and S6S_{6}.

  • •

    We apply a methodology inspired by Geiger et al. 2023 to use causal experiments to thoroughly test all of the properties of our proposed circuit.

  • •

    We survey current research in mechanistic interpretability and draw connections between the difficulty of our work and broader challenges in the field.

2 Related Work

Mechanistic Interpretability Interpreting and reverse engineering the mechanism used to complete a given task is an active field in interpretability. Analysis of such mechanisms and circuits are discovered mainly through a top-down approach of causal mediation analysis. In the previous work Hanna et al. 2023, Meng et al. 2023, Tigges et al. 2023, Wang et al. 2022b, the circuits are composed at the “component level” using the feed-forward layer and attention heads. We analyze the mechanisms of neural networks at the circuit level of individual and small groups of neurons, drawing directly on the work of Nanda et al. 2023a, Nanda et al. 2023b, Olah et al. 2020, Quirke & Barez 2024, Zhong et al. 2023, Zhang et al. 2023. Our work builds directly on “A Toy Model of Universality” by Chughtai et al. 2023. We recreated precisely their experimental setup for the groups S5S_{5} and S6S_{6}, though we came to different conclusions.

Grokking The models we study exhibit “grokking”, wherein the model first memorizes the training set and then much later generalizes to the held out data perfectly. Grokking was first identified by Power et al. 2022 and has been well studied for its counter-intuitive training dynamics [Kumar et al. 2023, Merrill et al. 2023, Varma et al. 2023, Rubin et al. 2023, Xu et al. 2023, Wei et al. 2022]. We conducted all the analysis on fully grokked models with perfect test accuracy, as models that show this behavior have often formed clean generalizing circuits that are more easily interpreted [Gromov 2023, Nanda et al. 2023a].

Group Theory We used many of the tools of group theory for our analysis, in particular the well-developed representation theory of the symmetric group. Tools for analyzing data on groups are well-laid out in Clausen & Baum 1993, Cohen & Welling 2016, Diaconis 1988, Kondor 2008, Kondor & Trivedi 2018, Huang et al. 2009, Karjol et al. 2023, Plumb et al. 2015.

3 Mathematical Preliminaries

This paper requires a familiarity with functions on groups, a topic that is uncommon in machine learning research. In this section we give an overview of the major concepts as they are realized in the permutation groups that we study. For a more formal introduction to group theory, please refer to Appendix D.

3.1 Permutations and the Symmetric Group

A permutation of nn elements is a map σ\sigma that sends one ordering of nn elements to a different ordering. For example the order-reversing permutation on four elements would be:

(1 2 3 4)↦σ(4 3 2 1)(1\;2\;3\;4)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sigma}}{{\mapsto}}(4\;3\;2\;1)

The identity permutation, denoted ee, leaves the ordering unchanged:

(1 2 3 4)↦e(1 2 3 4)(1\;2\;3\;4)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle e}}{{\mapsto}}(1\;2\;3\;4)

We refer to specific permutations by identifying them with the image of their action on the elements [n]≔{1,2,…,n}[n]\coloneqq\{1,2,\dots,n\} in increasing order. For the above example we would simply denote the order reversing permutation on four elements as (4 3 2 1)(4\;3\;2\;1).

We multiply two permutations on nn elements σ,τ\sigma,\tau by composition, read from right to left. If σ=(4 3 2 1)\sigma=(4\;3\;2\;1) and τ=(3 2 1 4)\tau=(3\;2\;1\;4), then σ​τ\sigma\tau is the permutation we obtain by first applying τ\tau and then applying σ\sigma to the output of τ\tau:

(1 2 3 4)↦τ(3 2 1 4)↦σ(4 1 2 3)(1\;2\;3\;4)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tau}}{{\mapsto}}(3\;2\;1\;4)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sigma}}{{\mapsto}}(4\;1\;2\;3)

First applying τ\tau and then σ\sigma has the same effect as just applying the permutation (4 1 2 3)(4\;1\;2\;3). Additionally every permutation σ\sigma has an inverse σ−1\sigma^{-1} such that σ​σ−1=e\sigma\sigma^{-1}=e. These properties makes all of the permutations on nn elements a group called the symmetric group, which we write SnS_{n}.

There are six permutations in S4S_{4} that do not change the position of 44:

(1 2 3 4)(2 1 3 4)(3 2 1 4)(1 3 2 4)(3 1 2 4)(2 3 1 4)\begin{matrix}(1\;2\;3\;4)&(2\;1\;3\;4)&(3\;2\;1\;4)\\ (1\;3\;2\;4)&(3\;1\;2\;4)&(2\;3\;1\;4)\end{matrix}

These six permutations form a subgroup of S4S_{4} because multiplication is closed within that subset, multiplying any two permutations that leave 44 unchanged results in another permutation that leaves 44 unchanged. You can see that these six permutations are isomorphic to S3S_{3} by simply “forgetting” about the 44 that is fixed in the fourth position. In the paper, we will refer to the subgroup of SnS_{n} isomorphic to Sn−1S_{n-1} that leaves element ii fixed as HiH_{i}.

One of the simplest types of permutations is a “transposition,” a permutation τ∈Sn\tau\in S_{n} that switches (“transposes”) two elements i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n] and leaves the remaining elements fixed. Every element of SnS_{n} can be decomposed into a product of transpositions. A given decomposition of a permutation is not unique, but the number of transpositions in the decomposition is an invariant of the permutation. For a permutation g∈Sng\in S_{n} if a set of transpositions τ1​τ2​…​τk=g\tau_{1}\tau_{2}\dots\tau_{k}=g, then every possible such set of transpositions will also have kk elements. The permutations that have an even number of transpositions are referred to as “even” permutations and those with an odd number are “odd.” The set of all even permutations in SnS_{n} is a subgroup referred to as the “alternating group” AnA_{n}.

If we take H4<S4H_{4}<S_{4} and multiply every element of on the left by some element σ∈S4\sigma\in S_{4} then we get a left coset of H4H_{4} denoted σ​H4\sigma H_{4}. The transposition τ=(4 2 3 1)\tau=(4\;2\;3\;1) switches the elements in the first and fourth positions. The elements of τ​H4\tau H_{4} are:

(4 2 3 1)(4 1 3 2)(4 2 1 3)(4 3 2 1)(4 1 2 3)(4 3 1 2)\begin{matrix}(4\;2\;3\;1)&(4\;1\;3\;2)&(4\;2\;1\;3)\\ (4\;3\;2\;1)&(4\;1\;2\;3)&(4\;3\;1\;2)\end{matrix}

This coset is characterized by every element having 44 in the first position. Every element of H4H_{4} has 44 in the fourth position and τ\tau switches the first and fourth positions. For any h∈H4h\in H_{4}, h​τh\tau has 44 in the first position because τ\tau moves it from the fourth. We would get a coset with all of the elements of S4S_{4} with 44 in the third position if we multiplied H4H_{4} on the left by the any permutation that switches three and four.

There are also right cosets where every element in a subgroup is multiplied from the right. The elements of H4​τH_{4}\tau are:

(4 2 3 1)(1 4 3 1)(3 2 4 1)(4 3 2 1)(3 4 2 1)(2 3 4 1)\begin{matrix}(4\;2\;3\;1)&(1\;4\;3\;1)&(3\;2\;4\;1)\\ (4\;3\;2\;1)&(3\;4\;2\;1)&(2\;3\;4\;1)\end{matrix}

This right coset is characterized by every element having 11 in the fourth position.

There are in fact four subgroups Hi<S4H_{i}<S_{4} that are isomorphic to S3S_{3}, one where each element {1,…,4}\{1,\dots,4\} is fixed. In general there are at least nn subgroups of SnS_{n} that are isomorphic to Sn−1S_{n-1}. Any two Hi,HjH_{i},\;H_{j} are conjugate to each other. Conjugation by an element σ\sigma maps x↦σ​x​σ−1x\mapsto\sigma x\sigma^{-1}. So if we have H4H_{4} and conjugate it by σ=(1 4 3 2)\sigma=(1\;4\;3\;2), then σ​H4​σ−1\sigma H_{4}\sigma^{-1} is H2H_{2}:

(1 2 3 4)(3 2 1 4)(4 2 3 1)(1 2 4 3)(4 2 1 3)(3 2 4 1)\begin{matrix}(1\;2\;3\;4)&(3\;2\;1\;4)&(4\;2\;3\;1)\\ (1\;2\;4\;3)&(4\;2\;1\;3)&(3\;2\;4\;1)\end{matrix}

If a subgroup is invariant to conjugation it is a normal subgroup. The only normal subgroup of SnS_{n} for n>4n>4 is the alternating group AnA_{n} of even permutations.

We will mostly refer to groups by name, but we will denote a general group as capital GG and a general subgroup as H≤GH\leq G. For a proper subgroup (H≠GH\neq G), we will write H<GH<G. For a normal subgroup, we will use N​⊴​GN\trianglelefteq G.

3.2 Fourier Transform over Groups

Though Group Fourier Transform is not central to our presentation of the coset circuit, it was an important tool that we used to analyze the the activations of the trained models. It is also a critical part of [Chughtai et al. 2023]. We introduce the concepts here and go over the the similarities and differences between our work and [Chughtai et al. 2023] in Section 7.

We begin with a presentation of the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), and then present the Group Fourier Transform by analogy. The DFT converts a function ff defined on {0,1,…,n−1}\{0,1,\dots,n-1\} to a complex-valued function via the formula:

f^(k)=∑t=0n−1f(t)e−2iπkt/n,k∈{0,…,n−1}\hat{f}(k)=\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}f(t)e^{-2i\pi kt/n},\quad k\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}

The DFT is commonly interpreted as a conversion from the time domain to the frequency domain because the e−2iπkt/ne^{-2i\pi kt/n} terms define a complex sinusoid with frequency 2​π​k​t/n2\pi kt/n. The frequency domain in this case means that these frequencies provide an alternative orthonormal basis from which we can work with functions. A function on {0,1,…,n−1}\{0,1,\dots,n-1\} can be represented as a vector f=(x0x1…xn−1)⊤f=\begin{pmatrix}x_{0}&x_{1}&\dots&x_{n-1}\end{pmatrix}^{\top} and its basis is given by the identity matrix InI_{n}. The DFT defines a basis transformation, much like any other. The Fourier basis is given nn vectors. The first basis vector, corresponding to k=0k=0, is all ones. The k=1k=1 basis vector is (1e−2iπ/n…e−2iπ(n−1)/n)\begin{pmatrix}1&e^{-2i\pi/n}&\dots&e^{-2i\pi(n-1)/n}\end{pmatrix}, and all of the rest for up to n−1n\!-\!1 are given by (1e−2iπk/n…e−2iπ(n−1)k/n)\begin{pmatrix}1&e^{-2i\pi k/n}&\dots&e^{-2i\pi(n-1)k/n}\end{pmatrix}.

The DFT has a particularly nice interpretation as a function on the cyclic group CnC_{n}, which is isomorphic to addition modulo nn. Please refer to Appendix D or to references such as [Diaconis 1988, Fulton & Harris, Joe 1991, Kondor 2008] for a more detailed discussion.

The interpretation of the DFT as being over the cyclic groups can be generalized to non-commutative groups. We go over the construction in Appendix E and F. The high level interpretation, however, is the same. For functions from Sn→ℂS_{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} there is an orthonormal basis that is equivariant to translations and convolutions. The frequencies for the Fourier transform over SnS_{n} are given by the partitions of nn. The “highest” frequencies can be interpreted as representing functions that are constant on permutations that all agree on a small number of elements of [n][n] [Ellis et al. 2017].

4 Model Architecture

As shown in Figure 1, the model we study contains separate left and right embeddings, followed by a fully connected linear layer with ReLU activations, and an unembedding layer. We use the same architecture as in [Chughtai et al. 2023] to enable consistent comparisons. 11 1 All code necessary for reproducing results and analysis is available at https://www.github.com/dashstander/sn-grok

  • •

    One hot vectors 𝐱g\mathbf{x}_{g} with length |G||G|.

  • •

    Two embedding matrices, 𝐄l,𝐄r\mathbf{E}_{l},\;\mathbf{E}_{r} with dimensions (d,|G|)(d,\;|G|), where dd is embedding dimension. SnS_{n} is non-abelian, i.e. not commutative, and the separate embeddings are to give the model extra capacity.

  • •

    A linear layer 𝐖\mathbf{W} with dimension (w, 2​d)(w,\;2d), ww denoting the width of the linear layer. After the linear layer we apply the ReLU pointwise nonlinearity.

  • •

    An unembedding layer 𝐔\mathbf{U} with dimension (|G|,w)(|G|,\;w), which transforms the outputs of the ReLU and linear layer to into logit space for the group.

We also note that the first dd columns of the linear layer will only act on the left embeddings and the second dd columns will only act on the right embeddings, so we can analyze 𝐖\mathbf{W} as the concatenation of two (w,d)(w,\;d) matrices: 𝐖=[𝐋​𝐑]\mathbf{W}=[\mathbf{L}\;\mathbf{R}].

𝐖​[𝐄l​𝐱g𝐄r​𝐱h]=𝐋𝐄l​𝐱g+𝐑𝐄r​𝐱h\mathbf{W}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{E}_{l}\mathbf{x}_{g}\\ \mathbf{E}_{r}\mathbf{x}_{h}\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf{L}\mathbf{E}_{l}\mathbf{x}_{g}+\mathbf{R}\mathbf{E}_{r}\mathbf{x}_{h}

Throughout the paper will refer to the values 𝐋𝐄l​𝐱g\mathbf{L}\mathbf{E}_{l}\mathbf{x}_{g}, 𝐑𝐄r​𝐱h\mathbf{R}\mathbf{E}_{r}\mathbf{x}_{h}, and their sum as “pre-activations” to denote that the ReLU activation function has not been applied. Post-ReLU values we refer to as “activations.”

5 Coset Circuits

5.1 Sign Neurons Implement the Sign Circuit

The even permutations form a subgroup called the alternating group AnA_{n}. The two cosets of AnA_{n} are the group itself and all of the odd permutations, τ​An\tau A_{n}. The multiplication of even and odd permutations has similar features to the addition of even and odd integers (hence the name). The sign map on a permutation in SnS_{n}, sgn\sign, is given by:

sgn⁡(σ)={1σ∈An−1σ∈τ​An\sign(\sigma)=\begin{cases}1\quad\sigma\in A_{n}\\ -1\quad\sigma\in\tau A_{n}\end{cases}

An “even” permutation that is in AnA_{n} is mapped to 11 and an “odd” permutation not in AnA_{n} is mapped to −1-1. For any σ,ρ∈Sn\sigma,\rho\in S_{n}, the sign of their product is the product of their signs: sgn⁡(σ​ρ)=sgn⁡(σ)​sgn⁡(ρ)\sign(\sigma\rho)=\sign(\sigma)\sign(\rho).

The one-layer model that we train uses this relationship to help solve the general group multiplication. Every single model we trained had at least two neurons dedicated to encoding the sign of the permutation product. Though the model cannot use the alternating group to completely solve multiplication in SnS_{n}, this sign circuit is emblematic of the general coset circuits the model forms.

Consider the neuron shown in Fig. 2. The left pre-activations are given by L⁡(σ)=sgn⁡(σ)L(\sigma)=\sign(\sigma) and the right pre-activations are R⁡(σ)=−sgn⁡(σ)R(\sigma)=-\sign(\sigma). The full action of the neuron is given by ReLU​(L⁡(σl)+R⁡(σr))\texttt{ReLU}(L(\sigma_{l})+R(\sigma_{r})) and there are three cases:

  1. 1.

    sgn⁡(σl)=sgn⁡(σr)⇒sgn⁡(σl​σr)=1\sign(\sigma_{l})=\sign(\sigma_{r})\Rightarrow\sign(\sigma_{l}\sigma_{r})=1. In this case L⁡(σl)L(\sigma_{l}) and R⁡(σr)R(\sigma_{r}) destructively interfere, cancelling out to 00. Both the pre-activation and activation are 00.

  2. 2.

    sgn⁡(σl)=−1,sgn⁡(σr)=1⇒sgn⁡(σl​σr)=−1\sign(\sigma_{l})=-1,\;\sign(\sigma_{r})=1\Rightarrow\sign(\sigma_{l}\sigma_{r})=-1. In this case L⁡(σl)L(\sigma_{l}) and R⁡(σr)R(\sigma_{r}) reinforce each other and sum to a positive value. Since 2>02>0, the activation value is 22.

  3. 3.

    sgn⁡(σl)=1,sgn⁡(σr)=−1⇒sgn⁡(σl​σr)=−1\sign(\sigma_{l})=1,\;\sign(\sigma_{r})=-1\Rightarrow\sign(\sigma_{l}\sigma_{r})=-1. Like in (2) the product σl​σr\sigma_{l}\sigma_{r} is an odd permutation and L⁡(σl)L(\sigma_{l}) and R⁡(σr)R(\sigma_{r}) constructively interfere, though this time L⁡(σl)+R⁡(σr)=−2L(\sigma_{l})+R(\sigma_{r})=-2, which is less than 00. Thus ReLU clips the pre-activation and sends it to 00.

5.2 Conjugate Subgroup Circuit

All four ways to multiply two cosets of AnA_{n} are well-defined. For each of the four options (even-even, odd-even, etc…) we know which coset of AnA_{n} the product will be in, but no other subgroup of SnS_{n} has this property. The model instead learns to use sets of conjugate subgroups. Recall that Hi<SnH_{i}<S_{n} is the subgroup isomorphic to Sn−1S_{n-1} that fixes the element i∈[n]i\in[n] in the ithi^{\text{th}} place and τi​j\tau_{ij} is the permutation that swaps ii and jj. Any two HiH_{i} and HjH_{j} are conjugate to each other, τi​j​Hi​τi​j=Hj\tau_{ij}H_{i}\tau_{ij}=H_{j} and τi​j​Hj​τi​j=Hi\tau_{ij}H_{j}\tau_{ij}=H_{i}. This means that there are two shared cosets between HiH_{i} and HjH_{j}, because Hi​τi​j=τi​j​HjH_{i}\tau_{ij}=\tau_{ij}H_{j} and Hj​τi​j=τi​j​HiH_{j}\tau_{ij}=\tau_{ij}H_{i}. The model implements the full group multiplication by picking out the shared cosets of conjugate subgroups.

As an example, consider a neuron that corresponds to H1H_{1} for the left permutation and H5H_{5} for the right permutation. The shared coset is H1​τ15=τ15​H5H_{1}\tau_{15}=\tau_{15}H_{5}, the set of all σ∈S5\sigma\in S_{5} with σ⁡(1)=5\sigma(1)=5. The pre-activations for the left and right permutations will be:

L⁡(σ)={4σ∈H12σ∈H1​τ120σ∈H1​τ13−2σ∈H1​τ14−4σ∈H1​τ15\displaystyle L(\sigma)=\begin{cases}4\quad\sigma\in H_{1}\\ 2\quad\sigma\in H_{1}\tau_{12}\\ 0\quad\sigma\in H_{1}\tau_{13}\\ -2\quad\sigma\in H_{1}\tau_{14}\\ -4\quad\sigma\in H_{1}\tau_{15}\\ \end{cases} R⁡(σ)={−4σ∈τ15​H5−2σ∈τ25​H50σ∈τ35​H52σ∈τ45​H54σ∈H5\displaystyle R(\sigma)=\begin{cases}-4\quad\sigma\in\tau_{15}H_{5}\\ -2\quad\sigma\in\tau_{25}H_{5}\\ 0\quad\sigma\in\tau_{35}H_{5}\\ 2\quad\sigma\in\tau_{45}H_{5}\\ 4\quad\sigma\in H_{5}\\ \end{cases} (1)

The final activation is still ReLU​(L⁡(σl)+R⁡(σr))\texttt{ReLU}(L(\sigma_{l})+R(\sigma_{r})), but now there are twenty-five possible pairs of cosets. All twenty-five combinations can be boiled down to two meaningful cases:

  1. 1.

    If L⁡(σl)+R⁡(σr)=0L(\sigma_{l})+R(\sigma_{r})=0, then σl​σr\sigma_{l}\sigma_{r} is in the shared coset H1​τ15H_{1}\tau_{15}.

  2. 2.

    If L⁡(σl)+R⁡(σr)≠0L(\sigma_{l})+R(\sigma_{r})\neq 0, then σl​σr\sigma_{l}\sigma_{r} is not in the shared coset H1​τ15H_{1}\tau_{15}.

Each left coset y​H5yH_{5} has a paired right coset H1​xH_{1}x such that H1​x​y​H5=H1​τ15=τ15​H5H_{1}xyH_{5}=H_{1}\tau_{15}=\tau_{15}H_{5}. The discrete values that LL and RR can take are precisely tuned so that those pairs of left and right cosets cancel out. Just like with the sign neuron, information about the pre-activation being negative is lost with the ReLU. This lost information has to be made up with extra neurons that correspond to (H1,H5)(H_{1},H_{5}) and assign different values to the cosets. For example, a different neuron that uses −L⁡(σl)−R⁡(σr)-L(\sigma_{l})-R(\sigma_{r}) will fail to fire for a different set of permutations. The combination

ReLU​(L⁡(σl)+R⁡(σr))+ReLU​(−L⁡(σl)−R⁡(σr))\texttt{ReLU}(L(\sigma_{l})+R(\sigma_{r}))+\texttt{ReLU}(-L(\sigma_{l})-R(\sigma_{r}))

will be much closer to a perfect on/off switch for coset membership.

5.3 Decoding Permutations with Coset Membership

There are n2n^{2} combinations of (Hi,Hj)(H_{i},H_{j}) subgroups. Each pair can be interpreted directly as encoding the set of permutations with ii in the j​thj\textsuperscript{th} position. Because of the way the coset neurons function, each neuron is better understood as firing when the value in the j​thj\textsuperscript{th} position is certainly not ii. The n2n^{2} combinations of (Hi,Hj)(H_{i},H_{j}) uniquely identify each element of SnS_{n}. We can use the outputs of twenty-five (Hi,Hj)(H_{i},H_{j}) neurons as a code that uniquely encodes each element of S5S_{5}. By analyzing the unembedding layer to see how the model makes use of (Hi,Hj)(H_{i},H_{j}) neurons, we see that this is almost exactly what the model does. This same construction works for every subgroup of SnS_{n} except for AnA_{n}.

6 The Process of Reverse Engineering

6.1 Identifying Coset Circuits

The first step in attempting to reverse engineer the mechanisms of a neural network is to spend some time staring at the weights and activations. Even a small one-layer model such as ours is too large to visualize all at once. It was not until we looked closely at the pre-ReLU activations that we produced a histogram similar to Figure 3. The left and right pre-activations of one neuron were nearly constant on the distinct cosets of the Frobenius group of order 20 (F20F_{20}), one of the subgroups of S5S_{5}. 22 2 F20F_{20} is equivalent to the group of affine transformations x↦a​x+bx\mapsto ax+b, where a,b,xa,b,x are in the field with five elements and a≠0a\neq 0. Further investigation revealed that almost every neuron had this property of only producing a discrete number of values that corresponded directly to the cosets of one of the subgroups of S5S_{5} or S6S_{6}. For a function f:G→ℝf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, we define CH​(f)C_{H}(f) to be the degree to which ff concentrates on the cosets H≤GH\leq G:

CH​(f)≔∑g​HVar⁡[f|g​H]Var⁡[f]C_{H}(f)\coloneqq\frac{\sum_{gH}\var[f|_{gH}]}{\var[f]}

Where Var⁡[f|g​H]\var[f|_{gH}] is the variance of ff when the domain is restricted to the coset g​HgH. Intuitively CH​(f)C_{H}(f) calculates the degree to which restricting to the cosets of HH reduces the variance of ff. If CH​(f)<1C_{H}(f)<1 it implies that the activations ff can meaningfully be understood better by looking at the values that it takes on the cosets of some subgroup. Recall that a single neuron is a function Ni:Sn×Sn→ℝN_{i}:S_{n}\times S_{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the sum of two functions G→ℝG\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, one for the left and right permutations, respectively. We can calculate min⁡CH\min C_{H} for each. Take as an example N115lN^{l}_{115}, the neuron shown in Figure 3. At 100,000 steps (on the far left) Var⁡[N115l]=5.23\var[N^{l}_{115}]=5.23. Its activations are not concentrated on the specific cosets of F20F_{20}, however, and CF20​(N115l)=2.96C_{F_{20}}(N^{l}_{115})=2.96. At 130,000 steps (on the far right) Var⁡[N115l]\var[N^{l}_{115}] has increased to 9.069.06, but CF20​(N115l)<10−5C_{F_{20}}(N^{l}_{115})<10^{-5}. The distribution within each coset of F20F_{20} has close to zero variance.

We see a typical example of what this looks like for the entire model in Fig. 4. As the validation loss approaches a small value, there is a rapid transition from the median coset concentration being approximately 11, to a minuscule value.

Even if it is apparent that a neuron is taking on discrete values and is a good candidate for being a coset neuron, it is difficult to tell by sight which subgroup the neuron is activating for. S5S_{5} and S6S_{6} only have 156 and 1,455 subgroups, respectively, 33 3 Sequence A005432 OEIS [OEIS Foundation Inc. 2023] so it is tractable to do an exhaustive search and calculate

argminH∈Sub⁡(G)⁡CH​(f)\argmin_{H\in\sub(G)}C_{H}(f)

the subgroup that minimizes the variance of ff for every neuron in the model. Running these calculations shows that for the 128 S5S_{5} models and 100 S6S_{6} models we trained over 99.2% of the neurons in the linear layer had minH∈Sub⁡(G)⁡CH​(f)<1.0\min_{H\in\sub(G)}C_{H}(f)<1.0, and the vast majority of those were less than 10−610^{-6}.

With the ability to calculate directly which neurons corresponded to which subgroup, our theories for exactly what the neurons were representing fell into place. The next step was to confirm that these neurons were actually responsible for the models’ performance.

6.2 Ablations

We have described how coset neurons function and how they can be identified. We will now show via ablations that coset neurons are not solely sufficient but also necessary to implement multiplication in SnS_{n}. We conduct ablations by removing neurons which have a coset concentration minH∈Sub⁡(G)⁡CH​(Ni)\min_{H\in\sub(G)}C_{H}(N_{i}) above a threshold.

If coset circuits are in fact responsible for the performance of our models, then we expect to see no change in the accuracy when the neurons that have not converged onto the cosets of a subgroup are removed from the model. This is precisely what we see on the far right of Figure 5. Of the 128 S5S_{5} models that we trained, 126 models saw no change in the accuracy when we removed the neurons with minH∈Sub⁡(G)⁡CH​(Ni)≥1\min_{H\in\sub(G)}C_{H}(N_{i})\geq 1 (the far right of Figure 5). Recall that if CH​(Ni)≥1C_{H}(N_{i})\geq 1, restricting to the cosets of HH at best does not change the variance of ff. Of the two models that did show a decrease in accuracy, they decreased to 99% and 98%.

We see more between-run variation when we remove more neurons. The median model has 24 out of 128 neurons with min⁡CH​(Ni)≥10−5\min C_{H}(N_{i})\geq 10^{-5}, but the 50th50^{\text{th}} and 25th25^{\text{th}} percentile accuracy is still 100%. It is not until we set the threshold to 10−610^{-6} that the 25th25^{\text{th}} percentile moves at all. When we set the threshold at 10−710^{-7} the performance for many models has collapsed, but the median model has had 42 neurons removed and the median accuracy is still 100%. Recall also that the neuron shown in the far right of Figure 3 has a coset concentration of 10−510^{-5}.

The overwhelming majority of neurons are identifiable as coset neurons. Of those neurons, those with the very highest concentration on cosets account for the largest portion of each model’s performance.

6.3 Causal Interventions

To rigorously test the properties of the coset circuit, we carefully designed causal experiments to test specific properties of in the circuits. We observe a circuit’s behavior over the entire data distribution (the full group SnS_{n}) and we see that our model of the circuit is consistent with the behavior of the true circuit. To confirm that our model of the circuit is correct, however, we need to “break” the circuit in targeted ways and test that it behaves in the way we predict. Neural circuits are complex enough that observational evidence is not enough. We aggregated runs over 128 S5S_{5} models of different and recorded their average loss and accuracy. Initially, over the initial models without intervention, we have accuracy extremely close to 1.

Embedding Exchange

The left and right embeddings encode different information—membership in right and left cosets, respectively—and cannot be interchanged. To test this we intervene to switch the left and right embeddings. After the intervention, we observed a significant drop in accuracy to 0 and a rise in loss. This aligns with our expectation that the membership is an important property that can’t be switched.

Switch Permutation Sign

The pre-activations are symmetric about the origin and the sign of the pre-activations does not matter, only whether or not the pre-activations is equal to zero. The relative sign of the left and right pre-activations should matter a lot. To test this, we have three tests: changing the sign of just the left embeddings, just the right embeddings, and both embeddings. In the case where we change both the sign and with commutative property, we can still expect the left and right activation to cancel out. Therefore, we should see a near-perfect accuracy and near-0 loss. The result is as expected. When we change the sign of only the left or right embedding, such cancellation law doesn’t hold anymore. Therefore, we observe a 0 accuracy in both cases.

Absolute Value Non-linearity

The circuit can create a perfect 0-1 coset membership switch with multiple neurons on constructive interference, but every single neuron is noisy and fundamentally limited by the ReLu non-linearity. To test this, we replace the ReLU activation function with the absolute value function x↦|x|x\mapsto|x|. We observe perfect accuracy and an even lower loss that a half of the original loss.

Distribution Change

It is essential to the functioning of each neuron that a large proportion of the pre-activations are close to zero. To test this we compare how adding noise from a 𝒩⁡(−1,1)\mathcal{N}(-1,1) and 𝒩⁡(1,1)\mathcal{N}(1,1) affect the performance of the model. We can see that changing the distribution of the activation in Perturb 𝒩⁡(−1,1)\mathcal{N}(-1,1) changes the performance less significantly than 𝒩⁡(1,1)\mathcal{N}(1,1). This indicates that the coset requires 0 as a threshold value to decide the membership.

7 The Group Composition via Representations Algorithm

Our experimental setup is identical to that of Chughtai et al. 2023, but our analysis led us to a different conclusion.Chughtai et al. 2023 proposed the “Group Composition via Representations” (GCR) algorithm. They show that, given an irrep ρ\rho of SnS_{n}, argmaxc∈Sntr[ρ(a)ρ(b)ρ(−1c)]=ab\argmax_{c\in S_{n}}\trace[\rho(a)\rho(b)\rho(^{-1}c)]=ab and propose that this is the algorithm the model is implementing. This requires that not only store the matrix irreps, but that the model perform the matrix multiplication within its mechanism. We find that most of the evidence [Chughtai et al. 2023] put forward is also consistent with coset circuits. The other evidence we were not able to independently replicate. We also find evidence that, to our understanding, is not consistent with the GCR algorithm but is explained by coset circuits.

7.1 Our Interpretation of the Evidence for GCR

Chughtai et al. 2023 put forward four main pieces of evidence, which we restate here for clarity: (1) Correlation between the model’s logits and characters of a learned representation ρ\rho. (2) The embedding and unembedding layers function as a “lookup table” for the representations of the input elements ρ⁡(a),ρ⁡(b)\rho(a),\;\rho(b) and the inverse of the target ρ⁡(c−1)\rho(c^{-1}). (3) The neurons in the linear layer calculate the matrix product ρ⁡(a)​ρ​(b)=ρ⁡(a​b)\rho(a)\rho(b)=\rho(ab). (4) Ablations showing that the circuit they identify is responsible for the majority of the model’s performance. Many of these points are equally consistent with the coset circuit and the other we could not find evidence for.

Ablations Though we do not perform all of the exact ablations that Chughtai et al. 2023 perform, we also find that the weights that show high Fourier concentration and perform the coset multiplication are integral to the model’s performance, see Section 6.2.

Irrep Look Up Table We were not able to find any evidence that the embedding or unembedding layers function as a look-up table for any representation except for the one-dimensional sign representation. We did find that the model’s weights and activations concentrate on specific irreps in the group Fourier basis. This is due, however, to concentration on cosets of specific subgroups, not because the matrix representations are realized anywhere in the weights. The relationship between functions that are constant on cosets and specific irreps is shown in Appendix G.2.

Logit Attribution The trace of a group representation is referred to as the “character” and often denoted χ\chi. We find that the model’s logits correlate with the character χρ​(a​b​c−1)\chi_{\rho}(abc^{-1}) when the irrep ρ\rho appears in the Fourier transform of the model’s weights. This is not, however, because the model has implemented the matrix product ρ⁡(a​b)​ρ​(c−1)\rho(ab)\rho(c^{-1}), but because the model is “counting” the number of cosets that a​bab and cc are both in. We prove in G.2, if the cosets are of conjugate subgroups that have their Fourier transform concentrated on the irrep ρ\rho (as we observe for the models in question), then the number of shared cosets will also correlate with the characters of ρ\rho.

Matrix Multiplication of Irreps We were not able to find any evidence that the linear layer implements matrix multiplication, again excluding scalar multiplication of the sign irrep.

7.2 Evidence GCR Does Not Explain

Concentration on Cosets In the standard basis the pre-activations of the overwhelming majority of neurons concentrate heavily on the cosets of subgroups. This is behavior is not predicted by the GCR algorithm.

The Difference Between Subgroups and Irreps The GCR algorithm and coset circuit cannot be equivalent because there is not, in fact, a one-to-one relationship between cosets and irreps. Most subgroups of SnS_{n} have their Fourier transforms concentrate on more than a single group (see Table 5 for the spectral properties of all of the subgroups of S5S_{5}), indeed this needs to be the case as there are many more subgroups than irreps. Please refer to Table 4 for a concrete comparison and Appendix 7.2 for an asymptotic analysis. We also observe coset circuits for some subgroups such as D10D_{10}44 4 The dihedral group of order 10, the symmetry group of a pentagon. will have coset circuits concentrated on both (3, 2)(3,\;2) or (2, 2, 1)(2,\;2,\;1), depending on the run. The GCR algorithm would treat these as different circuits, though their behavior is in fact identical.

Unembedding Correlations of Neurons We observe that the correlation between in the unembedding of neurons that concentrate on the same coset is on average 81.4%81.4\% (see Table 3). The correlation between neurons concentrated only on the same conjugacy class of subgroup (e.g. H1H_{1} and H2H_{2}) is on average −0.2%-0.2\%. The neurons that represent subgroups in the same conjugacy class will oftentimes, though not always, be concentrated on the same irrep. The model is treating cosets together but the irreps and conjugacy classes separately.

Coset Circuit Specific Causal Interventions The property that the loss goes down when we replace the ReLU activation function with absolute value is a very strange property that GCR does not predict.

The concentration of the model’s activations on irreps of SnS_{n} is striking evidence and the GCR algorithm that [Chughtai et al. 2023] detail could indeed solve the problem of group multiplication. The coset circuit is also consistent with all of the evidence that [Chughtai et al. 2023] provide and is additionally consistent with evidence that the GCR algorithm does not explain.

8 Discussion and Conclusion

We performed a circuit level analysis to discover the concrete mechanism a one layer fully connected network uses to solve group multiplication in S5S_{5} and S6S_{6}. We showed that the model decomposes S5S_{5} and S6S_{6} into its cosets and uses this structural information to perfectly implement the task.

Though our work concerns a toy problem, we highlight a core takeaway that applies broadly to the field of interpretability: we must treat proposed neural mechanisms as theories until they have been thoroughly tested.

When we identify what we believe to be a circuit within a larger network found via techniques such as [Conmy et al. 2023, Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2023], we have taken the first step towards mechanistically understanding how a model performs a task. The evidence we have for the circuit’s role in that task is, however, fundamentally observational and correlational. The nodes in the circuit’s computation graph are causally connected, but the relationship between the action of those nodes is only observed to be correlated to a certain task with respect to a distribution. This is valuable information to have, but the understanding that it imparts is limited and must be recognized as such.

When beginning this project we quickly noticed that the activations of sub-circuits of our model were concentrated on specific irreps of SnS_{n}. It was only with additional investigation that we were able to attach semantic meaning to this phenomenon. We observed that the neurons concentrated on a single irrep were activating for specific subgroups. The hypothesis of the coset circuits had formed, but it was still only a theory. The facts we had observed were incontrovertible, but their reason was unclear. It was only after performing the causal experiments detailed in Section 6.3 that we became confident we understood the mechanism. The simple reality is that more than one theory can be consistent with observational data, especially when that data only comes from a small subset of the full distribution. There is a long history of scholarship showing that interpretability techniques, including state-of-the-art, can give be misleading and contradictory results [Adebayo et al. 2020, Bolukbasi et al. 2021, Casper et al. 2023, Doshi-Velez & Kim 2017, Friedman et al. 2023, Hase et al. 2023, Jain & Wallace 2019, Makelov et al. 2023, McGrath et al. 2023].

In doing this work we had many advantages not available when interpreting real-world models: access to the entire distribution, an orthonormal basis for the function space of the network, and a relatively small model. The task of multiplication in SnS_{n} is deterministic and very well studied, we had many mathematical tools to bring to bear in analyzing the model. Even still, this project was quite challenging and the circuits we found surprised us. Interpreting real models will be even difficult. We encourage future work to apply interpretability tools cautiously and validate observational results with rigorous experimental tests.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to make the function and mechanisms of deep neural networks interpretable to humans. We present methods for reasoning about counterfactual and out of distribution behavior in the models that we train. Though our setting is too small to be directly relevant to real-world use cases, we hope that similar techniques will be able to test, audit, and monitor deep neural networks that have been deployed in the real world. We also present results that urge caution and humility when attempting to interpret neural networks. We believe that robust and effective interpretability techniques may mitigate some societal harms that could arise from the use of deep neural networks, but that mistakenly trusting illusory interpretability techniques could be disastrous.

Appendix B Structure of the Appendix

In the Appendix we provide more of the mathematical background needed to fully describe some of our results and techniques. In particular, we explain the Group Fourier Transform and how we used to to analyze our models. We do this because we believe it is of independent interest and also because it is necessary to fully explain where our results and those of Chughtai et al. 2023 diverge.

In Appendix C we go over the precise experimental set up of the models that we trained.

In Appendix D we introduce the necessary concepts from group theory needed to rigorously talk about the more mathematical aspects of our results.

In Appendix E we introduce representation theory, representations of the symmetric group, and the group Fourier transform.

In Appendix G we return to the coset circuit and coset neurons, with the presentation grounded in the mathematical concepts introduced in Appendices D and E.

Finally, in Appendix H we present extra graphs that did not fit in the main paper and in Appendix I we present a table of all of the conjugacy classes of subgroups of S5S_{5}.

Appendix C Experiment Details

We conducted experiments focusing on the permutation group of S5S_{5} and S6S_{6}. All models were trained on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 GPUs. All models were implemented in PyTorch Paszke et al. 2019 and trained with the Adam optimizer [Kingma & Ba 2014] with a fixed learning rate of 0.0010.001, weight decay set to 1.01.0, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 and β2=0.98\beta_{2}=0.98. At the beginning of each training run, the training set is sampled uniformly from all |Sn|2|S_{n}|^{2} combinations of permutations. Each optimization step was made on the entire training set. Using our setup a single S5S_{5} model trained in approximately 8 hours and a single S6S_{6} model trained in approximately 100 hours, though multiple training jobs could be scheduled on a single GPU. Analysis and reverse engineering was performed with Vink et al. 2023, Nanda & Bloom 2022, Harris et al. 2020, GAP, Stein et al. 2023.

Appendix D Group Theory

In this section, let us recall some basic definitions and propositions in group theory that are relevant to this paper.

D.1 Groups

A group GG is a nonempty set equipped with a special element e∈Ge\in G called the identity and a multiplication operator ⋅\cdot satisfying the following:

  • •

    (inverse) For each element a∈Ga\in G, there exists an element b∈Gb\in G such that a⋅b=b⋅a=ea\cdot b=b\cdot a=e.

  • •

    (identity) For each element a∈Ga\in G, a⋅e=e⋅a=aa\cdot e=e\cdot a=a.

  • •

    (associativity) For elements a,b,c∈Ga,b,c\in G, we have (a⋅b)⋅c=a⋅(b⋅c)(a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c).

The inverse of a∈Ga\in G is denoted by a−1a^{-1}.

Example D.1.

The set of integers ℤ\mathbb{Z} along with the addition ++ form a group. The identity element is 00. Also with the addition, the same is true for the set of rational numbers ℚ\mathbb{Q}, the set of real numbers ℝ\mathbb{R} and the set of complex numbers ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Example D.2.

The symmetric group introduced in Section 3.1 along with the composition of permutations satisfies the group axioms. The identity element is the identity permutation leaving each element unchanged.

Example D.3.

The set of natural numbers ℕ\mathbb{N} and addition do not form a group. The reason being that the inverse elements do not exist except for 00.

Definition D.4.

Given a group GG, a subgroup HH is a subset of GG such that

  • •

    a⋅b∈Ha\cdot b\in H for any a,b∈Ha,b\in H.

  • •

    e∈He\in H.

  • •

    a−1∈Ha^{-1}\in H.

One can check that HH along with the multiplication satisfies the group axiom as well. HH being a subgroup of GG is denoted by H≤GH\leq G.

D.2 Cosets and double cosets

Definition D.5.

Given a proper subgroup H<GH<G and an element g∈Gg\in G, the set g​H:={g​h|h∈H}gH:=\{gh~|~h\in H\} is called a left HH-coset. Similarly, H​g:={h​g|h∈H}Hg:=\{hg~|~h\in H\} is called a right HH-coset.

g​HgH is sometimes called a coset if the subgroup HH is clear from the context. When we do not mention whether it is a left coset or a right coset, left coset is the default.

Lemma D.6.

Two cosets g1​Hg_{1}H and g2​Hg_{2}H are either the same subset of GG or disjoint (i.e., g1​H​⋂g2​H=∅g_{1}H\bigcap g_{2}H=\emptyset).

Lemma D.7.

If GG is a finite group, any two HH-cosets have the same number of elements.

As a result, one can pick suitable representative elements (but not unique) g1,⋯,gn∈Gg_{1},\cdots,g_{n}\in G, so that g1​H,⋯,gn​Hg_{1}H,\cdots,g_{n}H form a partition of GG. Because the cosets have equal sizes, we can also conclude that |G||G| is always divisible by |H||H|.

Definition D.8.

Given two subgroups H,L<GH,L<G and an element g∈Gg\in G, the set HgL:={hgl|h∈H,l∈L}HgL:=\{hgl~|~h\in H,l\in L\} is called the (H,L)(H,L)-double coset, or the double coset if the pair (H,L)(H,L) is clear from the context.

Double cosets enjoy the similar property as cosets:

Lemma D.9.

Two double cosets H​g1​LHg_{1}L and H​g2​LHg_{2}L are either the same or disjoint.

As a result, GG can be similarly decomposed as a disjoint union of (H,L)(H,L)-double cosets. However, when GG is finite, (H,L)(H,L)-double cosets do not always come with equal sizes. So the decomposition is not equal-sized.

For simplicity, we call the (H,H)(H,H)-double coset the HH-double coset.

D.3 Normal Subgroups

Definition D.10.

A subgroup NN is normal in GG, denoted N​⊴​GN\trianglelefteq G, if for any g∈Gg\in G and any n∈Nn\in N, we have g​n​g−1∈Ngng^{-1}\in N.

A subgroup is normal if and only if the left and right cosets are the same, i.e., for any g∈G,g​N=N​gg\in G,\ gN=Ng. Normal subgroups are important because they are precisely the groups for which the set of NN-cosets G/NG/N has a natural group structure.

Definition D.11.

Given a group GG and a normal subgroup N​⊴​GN\trianglelefteq G, the quotient group G/NG/N is defined to be the set of NN-cosets endowed with the multiplication given by g​N⋅h​N=g​h​NgN\cdot hN=ghN for any g,h∈Gg,h\in G.

The well-definedness of the multiplication is a consequence of NN being normal and its group axioms are straightforward to check.

Example D.12.

If GG is commutative (for every g,h∈Gg,h\in G, we have g​h=h​ggh=hg), every subgroup H≤GH\leq G is normal.

Example D.13.

If G=SnG=S_{n}, the subgroup Sn−1S_{n-1} fixing the first element is not a normal subgroup. On the other hand, the alternating subgroup AnA_{n} (consisting of even permutations) is a normal subgroup of SnS_{n}.

The double cosets of a normal subgroup are simply the usual cosets.

Lemma D.14.

Given a normal subgroup H​⊴​GH\trianglelefteq G, the left HH-coset and the right HH-coset are in one-to-one correspondence. Furthermore, the set of HH-double cosets is also in one-to-one correspondence to HH-cosets.

Proof.

By definition, g​H​g−1=HgHg^{-1}=H. Therefore, g​H=H​ggH=Hg. H​g​H=g​H​H=g​HHgH=gHH=gH. ∎

D.4 Conjugate Subgroups

The cosets of a normal subgroup N​⊴​GN\trianglelefteq G themselves form a group. If x,y∈Gx,\;y\in G and x∈g​Nx\in gN but y∈h​N\;y\in hN, then x​y∈g​h​Nxy\in ghN. If GG is not abelian, however, many or even all subgroups are not normal and do not have this property. For a non-normal subgroup HH, a g∉Hg\notin H gives rise to a different conjugate subgroup g​H​g−1gHg^{-1}.

In general, the relationship between the cosets of HH and g​H​g−1gHg^{-1} is complex, but they will have at least one left and one right coset in common: H​g−1=g−1​(g​H​g−1)Hg^{-1}=g^{-1}(gHg^{-1}). Every right coset H​xHx will have a left coset pair y⁡(g​H​g−1)y(gHg^{-1}) such that when multiplied, right coset on the left and left coset on the right, H​x​y​(g​H​g−1)=H​g−1Hxy(gHg^{-1})=Hg^{-1}, specifically when x​y=g−1xy=g^{-1}.

This relationship between the cosets of pairs of conjugate subgroups is not as powerful as that of the cosets of normal subgroups, but conjugate subgroups are guaranteed to exist in non-abelian groups, whereas there are many simple groups without normal subgroups at all.

This relationship between pairs of conjugate subgroups is also useful enough that it is used by every model we trained. In general, we have the following:

Lemma D.15.

For any H≤GH\leq G and an element g∈Gg\in G, the set of conjugate elements g​H​g−1gHg^{-1} forms a subgroup of GG.

If the conjugate subgroup g​H​g−1gHg^{-1} is different than HH, the left and right cosets g​H,H​ggH,Hg are different.

The double coset circuits operate by first identifying a pair of different conjugate subgroups HH and g​H​g−1gHg^{-1}. It exploits the fact that the left coset g​HgH and the right coset (g​H​g−1)​g(gHg^{-1})g are the same subset of GG, which will be fully generalized and elaborated in the later sections.

D.5 An important case

When a group GG decomposes as only two disjoint HH-double cosets, any pair of subgroups conjugate to HH shares a left coset with another’s right coset.

Lemma D.16.

Let H1,…,HnH_{1},...,H_{n} be conjugate subgroups of GG, such that for each HiH_{i} the double coset Hi​g​HiH_{i}gH_{i} is equal to either HiH_{i} or G∖HiG\setminus H_{i}. Then for each pair of subgroups HiH_{i} and HjH_{j} there exists a g∈Gg\in G such that Hi​g=g​HjH_{i}g=gH_{j}. Moreover, the only double cosets of HiH_{i} and HjH_{j} are Hi​g​Hj=g​HjH_{i}gH_{j}=gH_{j} and Hi​x​Hj=G∖g​HjH_{i}xH_{j}=G\setminus gH_{j}.

Proof.

If i=ji=j, for any h∈Hih\in H_{i} the shared coset is the subgroup itself. If i≠ji\neq j, because HiH_{i} and HjH_{j} are conjugate, there exists a g∈Gg\in G such that Hj=g−1​Hi​gH_{j}=g^{-1}H_{i}g. The left coset is equal to the right coset:

g​Hj=g⁡(g−1​Hi​g)=Hi​ggH_{j}=g(g^{-1}H_{i}g)=H_{i}g

Notice that the double coset Hi​g​Hj=Hi​(Hi​g)=Hi​gH_{i}gH_{j}=H_{i}(H_{i}g)=H_{i}g. But for x≠gx\neq g:

Hi​x​Hj\displaystyle H_{i}xH_{j} =Hi​x​g−1​Hi​g\displaystyle=H_{i}xg^{-1}H_{i}g (2)
=(G∖Hi)​g\displaystyle=(G\setminus H_{i})g (3)
=G∖Hi​g\displaystyle=G\setminus H_{i}g (4)

∎

Appendix E Representation Theory

E.1 Preliminaries

Definition E.1.

Given a group GG, a representation of GG is a group homomorphism ρV:G→G​L​(V)\rho_{V}:G\rightarrow GL(V) for some finite (but nonzero) dimensional vector space VV over a field kk. When we do not specifically mention kk, we use ℂ\mathbb{C} as the default.

In other words, a representation maps a group element gg to a linear operator f⁡(g):V→Vf(g):V\rightarrow V where VV is a vector space of dimension dd, so that the group multiplication becomes compositions of linear operators (f⁡(g⋅h)=f⁡(g)∘f⁡(h)f(g\cdot h)=f(g)\circ f(h)). Without explicit specifications, all representations in this paper are assumed to be over complex numbers. Recall also that finite dimensional linear operators can be represented as matrices, and composition of linear operators is then given as matrix multiplication.

When the context is clear, sometimes we omit the subscript VV in the notation ρV\rho_{V}.

The representations of finite groups have a rich and beautiful theory (see Diaconis 1988, Fulton & Harris, Joe 1991). Here, we recall a few basic definitions and facts without going into details.

Definition E.2.

A representation ρV:G→G​L​(V)\rho_{V}:G\rightarrow GL(V) is a sub-representation of ρW:G→G​L​(W)\rho_{W}:G\rightarrow GL(W) if VV can be identified as a linear subspace of WW so that ρW​(g)\rho_{W}(g) restricts to ρV​(g)\rho_{V}(g) for all g∈Gg\in G.

Example E.3.

For any group GG, the map G→G​L​(V)G\rightarrow GL(V) sending all elements to the identity matrix is a representation. When dim​(V)=1\text{dim}(V)=1, we call it the trivial representation of GG.

Definition E.4.

Given two representations ρV,ρW\rho_{V},\rho_{W} of GG, the direct sum of vector spaces V⊕WV\oplus W admits a natural representation of GG by letting ρV,ρW\rho_{V},\rho_{W} act on each component separately. We call this the direct sum of representations ρV,ρW\rho_{V},\rho_{W}, and denote it by ρV⊕ρW\rho_{V}\oplus\rho_{W}.

Definition E.5.

Similarly, given two representations ρV,ρW\rho_{V},\rho_{W}, the tensor product V⊗WV\otimes W admits a natural representation of GG by acting on V,WV,W separately and extend by linearity. We call this the tensor product of representations ρV,ρW\rho_{V},\rho_{W}, and denote it by ρV⊗ρW\rho_{V}\otimes\rho_{W}.

Definition E.6.

A representation ρ\rho of a group GG is irreducible, if it does not have sub-representations other than ρ\rho.

We denote the set of all irreducible representations of GG by Irr⁡(G)\irr(G)

Lemma E.7.

A representation ρ\rho of a finite group GG is a direct sum of irreducible representations.

Example E.8.

The trivial representation of GG is irreducible.

Example E.9.

The permutation representation maps Sn→G​L​(ℂ3)S_{n}\rightarrow GL(\mathbb{C}^{3}), i.e. ×33\!\times\!3 matrices with a single 11 in each row and column and zeros everywhere else.

(2 1 3)↦(010100001)(3 2 1)↦(001010100)(2\;1\;3)\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&0&1\\ \end{pmatrix}\quad(3\;2\;1)\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ \end{pmatrix}

You can see that the matrices of the permutation representation act on the basis vectors of ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3}:

(001010100)​(xyz)=(zyx)\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}z\\ y\\ x\end{pmatrix}

What it means to be a representation is that the group multiplication becomes matrix multiplication, so just as (2 1 3)​(3 2 1)=(2 3 1)(2\;1\;3)(3\;2\;1)=(2\;3\;1),

(010100001)​(001010100)=(001100010)\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&0&1\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\end{pmatrix}
Example E.10.

The permutation representation is reducible, because there is a subspace of ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} that is invariant to it’s action.

(001010100)​(xxx)=(xxx)\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\ x\\ x\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\ x\\ x\end{pmatrix}

Note that there is no permutation matrix acting on the vector (xxx)T\begin{pmatrix}x&x&x\end{pmatrix}^{T} that will change it, because all of the components are equal.

As it turns out, there are no irreducible representations of S3S_{3} that are three-dimensional. The largest irrep of S3S_{3} is ρ(2,1)\rho_{(2,1)}, which is made of ×22\!\times\!2 matrices. The matrices of the (2,1)(2,1) irrep of S3S_{3} are as follows:

(1 2 3)\displaystyle(1\;2\;3) ↦(1001)\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} (2 1 3)\displaystyle(2\;1\;3) ↦(−1001)\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} (3 2 1)\displaystyle(3\;2\;1) ↦(1/2−3/23/2−1/2)\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1/2&-\sqrt{3}/2\\ \sqrt{3}/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}
(1 3 2)\displaystyle(1\;3\;2) ↦(−1/23/23/21/2)\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}-1/2&\sqrt{3}/2\\ \sqrt{3}/2&1/2\end{pmatrix} (3 1 2)\displaystyle(3\;1\;2) ↦(−1/23/2−3/2−1/2)\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}-1/2&\sqrt{3}/2\\ -\sqrt{3}/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix} (2 3 1)\displaystyle(2\;3\;1) ↦(−1/23/2−3/2−1/2)\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}-1/2&\sqrt{3}/2\\ -\sqrt{3}/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}

We leave it as an exercise to the reader to verify that ρ(2,1)​(2 1 3)​ρ(2,1)​(3 2 1)=ρ(2,1)​(2 3 1)\rho_{(2,1)}(2\;1\;3)\rho_{(2,1)}(3\;2\;1)=\rho_{(2,1)}(2\;3\;1).

Trace is an important notion in linear algebra. Taking trace of a representation induces an important map from GG to ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Definition E.11.

Let ρV\rho_{V} be a representation of GG. The character of ρV\rho_{V} is a map χ⁡(ρV):G→ℂ\chi(\rho_{V}):G\rightarrow\mathbb{C} given by χ⁡(ρV)​(g)=tr⁡(ρV​(g))\chi(\rho_{V})(g)=\trace(\rho_{V}(g)).

Lemma E.12.

The character χ⁡(ρV)\chi(\rho_{V}) takes the same value on a conjugacy class of GG. In other words, χ⁡(ρV)​(h)=χ⁡(ρV)​(g​h​g−1)\chi(\rho_{V})(h)=\chi(\rho_{V})(ghg^{-1}).

To distill this property for a wider range of functions, we have the following definition:

Definition E.13.

Let f:G→ℂf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{C} be a map. If f⁡(h)=f⁡(g​h​g−1)f(h)=f(ghg^{-1}) for any g,h∈Gg,h\in G, ff is called a class function.

For a finite group GG, the set of class functions form a finite-dimensional vector space. There is an important inner product between class functions.

Definition E.14.

The inner product of two class functions ϕ,ψ\phi,\psi are defined as:

⟨ϕ,ψ⟩=1|G|​∑g∈Gϕ⁡(g)​ψ⁡(g)¯.\langle\phi,\psi\rangle=\dfrac{1}{|G|}\sum\limits_{g\in G}\phi(g)\overline{\psi(g)}.

As we require the class functions to take the same values on conjugacy classes, the dimension of the vector space of class functions is equal to the number of conjugacy classes in GG. On the other hand, we have the following important theorem:

Theorem E.15.

The characters of Irr⁡(G)\irr(G) forms an orthonormal basis in the vector space of class functions.

Lemma E.16.

For a finite group GG, Irr⁡(G)\irr(G) is a finite set. Furthermore, the order of Irr⁡(G)\irr(G) is equal to the number of conjugacy classes in GG.

Appendix F Fourier transform over finite groups

Despite being mostly perceived as a powerful tool in physics and engineering, the Fourier transform has also been successfully applied in group theory thanks to its generalization to locally compact abelian groups as well as an analog over finite groups. The purpose the group Fourier transform serves is largely analogous to the one served by the classical Fourier transform: it provides an alternate orthogonal basis with which to analyze functions from a group GG to either ℝ\mathbb{R} or ℂ\mathbb{C}.

To motivate the transition from the classical Fourier theory to the Fourier theory over groups, we start with a brief recall of the definitions.

The classical Fourier transform over real numbers converts a complex-valued Lebesgue-integrable function f:ℝ→ℂf:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} into a function from the complex unit circle S1S^{1} to ℂ\mathbb{C} with following formula:

f^​(ξ)=∫−∞∞f⁡(x)​e−2​π​i​ξ​x​𝑑x.\hat{f}(\xi)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)e^{-2\pi i\xi x}dx. (5)

Taking one step further in abstraction, we note that e−2​π​i​ξ​xe^{-2\pi i\xi x} as a function of xx has the defining properties of turning additions into multiplications (being a group homomorphism) and always having complex norm 11:

e−2​π​i​ξ​(x1+x2)\displaystyle e^{-2\pi i\xi(x_{1}+x_{2})} =e−2​π​i​ξ​x1⋅e−2​π​i​ξ​x2,\displaystyle=e^{-2\pi i\xi x_{1}}\cdot e^{-2\pi i\xi x_{2}},
|e−2​π​i​ξ​x|\displaystyle|e^{-2\pi i\xi x}| =1.\displaystyle=1.

We call such functions the characters of ℝ\mathbb{R}, though they are often thought of as frequencies. One can prove that all characters of ℝ\mathbb{R} can be written as e−2​π​i​ξ​xe^{-2\pi i\xi x} for a suitable ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R}.

Looking back at (5), the properties we need in order to define the Fourier transform over ℝ\mathbb{R} are:

  • •

    ℝ\mathbb{R} has the Lebesgue measure (allowing for integration to happen).

  • •

    ℝ\mathbb{R} is a group (so that the characters make sense as group homomorphisms from ℝ\mathbb{R} to the unit circle group S1⊂ℂS^{1}\subset\mathbb{C}).

Now, if we are given a finite group GG, the Fourier transform of a finite group is an operator converting a map f:G→ℂf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{C} into a function between Irr⁡(G)\irr(G) and the set of linear operators M⁡(V)M(V).

Definition F.1.

Given a group GG, the Fourier transform of a map f:G→ℂf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{C} is a function f^\hat{f} from Irr⁡(G)\irr(G) to the union of M⁡(ℂn)M(\mathbb{C}^{n}) for all nn such that

f^​(ρ)=∑a∈Gf⁡(a)​ρ​(a)\hat{f}(\rho)=\sum\limits_{a\in G}f(a)\rho(a)

for an irreducible representation ρ\rho.

The analogy comes from the following similar facts:

  • •

    GG, as a finite set, has the invariant discrete measure (where the “integration” becomes the sum).

  • •

    GG is a group, and the irreps ρ\rho are in a sense the ”smallest” group homomorphisms from GG to G​L​(n,ℂ)GL(n,\mathbb{C}) (note that the images of ρ\rho similarly have complex-norm-11 determinants due to GG being a finite group).

For more details and applications, one can refer to, for example, Elias M. Stein 2003. We would like to note that there is also an inverse transform that restores the original function ff from f^\hat{f}:

f⁡(g)=1|G|​∑ρ∈Irr⁡(G)dρ​tr⁡[f^​(ρ)​ρ​(g−1)]f(g)=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{\rho\in\irr(G)}d_{\rho}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho)\rho(g^{-1})] (6)

Appendix G The Coset Circuit (with more math)

We did not introduce it in the main body of our paper because it would distract from the core of our results, but for the first half of our investigation the Fourier transform over the symmetric group was integral to our investigation. We were building directly on [Chughtai et al. 2023] who had shown striking results around the weights of single-layer models showing high degrees of correlation with the irreps of the symmetric group. We wished to cast those results in the language of the group Fourier transform. Even when we realized that the mechanism of the model was based around cosets it became extremely important to understand why our coset circuit was so concentrated in Fourier space.

G.1 Harmonic Analysis on the Symmetric Group

The presentation in the Appendix E was given in terms of functions on ℂ\mathbb{C} because it is required for arbitrary groups. For SnS_{n} all of the irreps are rational [Fulton & Harris, Joe 1991] and the Fourier transform of functions on SnS_{n} can safely be defined over ℝ\mathbb{R}.

In this section we describe how we use the Fourier transform to analyze the weights and activations of an MLP. The inputs to the model are two one-hot vectors, 𝐱l,𝐱r\mathbf{x}_{l},\;\mathbf{x}_{r}, which multiply the embedding matrices 𝐄l​𝐱l\mathbf{E}_{l}\mathbf{x}_{l} and 𝐄r​𝐱r\mathbf{E}_{r}\mathbf{x}_{r}. 𝐄l\mathbf{E}_{l} and 𝐄r\mathbf{E}_{r} are d×|G|d\times|G| matrices, where dd is the embedding dimension and |G||G| is the size of the group. The columns are the embedding vectors for a single element g∈Gg\in G. The normal approach would be to try and look at the column spaces of 𝐄l\mathbf{E}_{l} and 𝐄r\mathbf{E}_{r}, as these columns are the inputs to the model. However, since each row of 𝐄l\mathbf{E}_{l} and 𝐄r\mathbf{E}_{r} and each value of that row is associated with a single element of GG, we instead treat each row of the embedding as a function f:G→ℝf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{R}.

In fact, anywhere in the model where a matrix or set of activations has |G||G| in the shape we can expand into the Fourier basis. For non-abelian groups, each Fourier frequency is an irrep, and the Fourier transform for each irrep is matrix-valued. This is, on its face, less interpretable than what we started with. Following the techniques outlined in Diaconis 1988, however, we can expand the function at each element g∈Gg\in G into a new Fourier basis. Concretely, if our function f:G→ℝf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is represented as a vector, we know from 6 that each element of the vector is a sum of the Fourier components:

[f⁡(g1)f⁡(g2)f⁡(g|G|)]=1|G|​[∑ρdρ​tr⁡[f^​(ρ)​ρ​(g1−1)]∑ρdρ​tr⁡[f^​(ρ)​ρ​(g2−1)]∑ρdρ​tr⁡[f^​(ρ)​ρ​(g|G|−1)]]\begin{bmatrix}f(g_{1})\\ f(g_{2})\\ \vdots\\ f(g_{|G|})\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{|G|}\begin{bmatrix}\sum_{\rho}d_{\rho}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho)\rho(g^{-1}_{1})]\\ \sum_{\rho}d_{\rho}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho)\rho(g^{-1}_{2})]\\ \vdots\\ \sum_{\rho}d_{\rho}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho)\rho(g^{-1}_{|G|})]\end{bmatrix}

We can keep track of all of the Fourier components at once by purposefully not completing the sum from 6), but instead keep each term into a new dimension:

1|G|​[dρ1​tr⁡[f^​(ρ1)​ρ1​(g1−1)]…dρk​tr⁡[f^​(ρk)​ρk​(g1−1)]dρ1​tr⁡[f^​(ρ1)​ρ1​(g2−1)]…dρk​tr⁡[f^​(ρk)​ρk​(g2−1)]dρ1​tr⁡[f^​(ρ1)​ρ1​(g|G|−1)]…dρk​tr⁡[f^​(ρk)​ρk​(g|G|−1)]]\frac{1}{|G|}\begin{bmatrix}d_{\rho_{1}}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho_{1})\rho_{1}(g^{-1}_{1})]&\dots&d_{\rho_{k}}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho_{k})\rho_{k}(g^{-1}_{1})]\\ d_{\rho_{1}}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho_{1})\rho_{1}(g^{-1}_{2})]&\dots&d_{\rho_{k}}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho_{k})\rho_{k}(g^{-1}_{2})]\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ d_{\rho_{1}}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho_{1})\rho_{1}(g^{-1}_{|G|})]&\dots&d_{\rho_{k}}\trace[\hat{f}(\rho_{k})\rho_{k}(g^{-1}_{|G|})]\\ \end{bmatrix}

Though this may seem like it is only making the data more complicated, it gives us many tools for analyzing the data. In particular, it turns out that the weights and activations are sparse in this new basis, which gives us a small path forward in analyzing the mechanisms.

Corollary G.1.

If HiH_{i} and HjH_{j} are conjugate subgroups of GG such that the only two double cosets are Hi​g​HjH_{i}gH_{j} and Hi​HjH_{i}H_{j}, then each right coset Hi​xH_{i}x has a paired left coset y​HjyH_{j} where y=x−1​gy=x^{-1}g such that for all hx∈Hi​xh_{x}\in H_{i}x and hy∈y​Hjh_{y}\in yH_{j}, hx​hy∈Hi​g​Hjh_{x}h_{y}\in H_{i}gH_{j}

Lemma G.2.

Let f:G→ℂf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{C} be constant on the cosets of H≤GH\leq G and non-zero on at least one coset. Then f^​(ρ)=0\hat{f}(\rho)=0 if the restriction of ρ\rho to HH, ρ|H\rho|_{H} does not contain the trivial representation as a subrepresentation.

Proof.

The function ff can be decomposed as the sum of functions

fx​H​(σ)={αxσ∈x​H0otherwisef_{xH}(\sigma)=\begin{cases}\alpha_{x}\quad\sigma\in xH\\ 0\quad\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

for each coset x​HxH. Because Fourier transform f^\hat{f} is invariant under translation we may, without loss of generality, analyze only the function fHf_{H}. For a given αx\alpha_{x}, f^x​H​(ρ)=f^Hx​(ρ)=ρ⁡(x)​f^H​(ρ)\hat{f}_{xH}(\rho)=\hat{f}^{x}_{H}(\rho)=\rho(x)\hat{f}_{H}(\rho) for all x∈Gx\in G. Recall the definition of f^H​(ρ)\hat{f}_{H}(\rho) from F.1:

f^H​(ρ)\displaystyle\hat{f}_{H}(\rho) =∑g∈GfH​(g)​ρ​(g)\displaystyle=\sum_{g\in G}f_{H}(g)\rho(g) (7)
=αH​∑h∈Hρ|H​(h)\displaystyle=\alpha_{H}\sum_{h\in H}\rho|_{H}(h) (8)
=αH​∑h∈HT−1​[⨁τi∈𝒯τi​(h)]​T\displaystyle=\alpha_{H}\sum_{h\in H}T^{-1}[\bigoplus_{\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{T}}\tau_{i}(h)]T (9)
=αH​T−1​[⨁τi∈𝒯∑h∈Hτi​(h)]​T\displaystyle=\alpha_{H}T^{-1}[\bigoplus_{\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{h\in H}\tau_{i}(h)]T (10)

where in 9 we decompose ρ|H\rho|_{H} into a direct sum of irreps of HH. But because each τi\tau_{i} is irreducible, ∑h∈Hτi​(h)=𝟎\sum_{h\in H}\tau_{i}(h)=\mathbf{0} unless τi\tau_{i} is the trivial irrep. Thus, unless the decomposition of ρH\rho_{H} into irreps of HH includes the trivial representation, f^|H=0\hat{f}|_{H}=0 ∎

G.2 Logits and Counting Cosets

In Chughtai et al. 2023, one way of justifying the GCR algorithm is to study the correlation between the character functions and the neuron activations. We would like to argue that the correlation between the GCR and the coset membership counting function may already exist, and in some simple cases it can be made explicit.

More precisely, we are measuring the correlation between the character function χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) of an irrep ρ\rho with a set function f:G→ℂf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{C}. In this section, we provide an explicit characterization of ff in terms of trace and irreps, when ff counts the membership of cosets.

We are specifically interested in the following situation:

Lemma G.3.

Suppose f:G→ℂf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{C} is a function such that its Fourier transform f^\hat{f} is nonzero only on an irreducible representation ρ\rho and the trivial representation. Let f^​(ρ)=A∈M⁡(ℂn)\hat{f}(\rho)=A\in M(\mathbb{C}^{n}). We have the following explicit formula:

f⁡(σ)=dρ|G|​tr⁡(A⋅ρ⁡(σ−1))+|H||G|.f(\sigma)=\dfrac{d_{\rho}}{|G|}\trace(A\cdot\rho(\sigma^{-1}))+\dfrac{|H|}{|G|}. (11)
Proof.

This is immediate by the Fourier inversion formula. ∎

In this case, although ff is not directly written in terms of tr⁡(ρ⁡(σ−1))\trace(\rho(\sigma^{-1})), ff is correlated with tr⁡(ρ⁡(σ−1))\trace(\rho(\sigma^{-1})) depending on how much AA is concentrated to the diagonal and how even are the diagonal entries. For the rest of the section, we show that under certain conditions, Equation (11) applies verbatim to the functions that count membership of cosets for a collection of conjugate subgroups.

Given a subgroup H≤GH\leq G, let 1H1_{H} be the function that takes value 11 on the subgroup HH, and takes 00 otherwise. The action of GG on cosets G/HG/H induces a representation of GG on ℂ|G/H|\mathbb{C}^{|G/H|} by permuting the basis accordingly. We call it the permutation representation of GG on G/HG/H.

Lemma G.4.

The Fourier transform of 1H1_{H} is nonzero only at the irreducible components of the permutation representation of GG on G/HG/H.

Proof.

By definition, the Fourier transform of 1H1_{H} on an irrep ρ\rho is

1H^​(ρ)=∑a∈Hρ⁡(a).\widehat{1_{H}}(\rho)=\sum\limits_{a\in H}\rho(a).

Notice that the image of ∑a∈Hρ⁡(a)\sum\limits_{a\in H}\rho(a) are invariant under HH due to the symmetry of this expression.

Let VV be the vector space where ρ\rho acts on. Under the action of the subgroup HH through ρ\rho, one can decompose VV as irreps of HH. We group them into two parts:

V=VH⊕V′,V=V^{H}\oplus V^{\prime},

where VHV^{H} is a direct sum of copies of trivial representation of HH (or in other words, the invariant subspace of VV under HH), and V′V^{\prime} is the direct sum of nontrivial irreducible components of VV.

We immediately see the following by definition:

∑a∈Hρ⁡(a)|VH=|H|⋅IdVH.\sum\limits_{a\in H}\rho(a)|_{V^{H}}=|H|\cdot\text{Id}_{V^{H}}.

Also by definition, nontrivial irreps of HH do not have invariant subspaces since they do not admit proper sub-representations. Therefore,

∑a∈Hρ⁡(a)|V′=0.\sum\limits_{a\in H}\rho(a)|_{V^{\prime}}=0.

As a result, 1H^​(ρ)\widehat{1_{H}}(\rho) is simply a scaled projection to the invariant subspace of VV. Whether it is zero depends on whether ResH​ρ\text{Res}_{H}\rho has any trivial components.

By Frobenius reciprocity,

⟨IndHG​(1H),χ⁡(ρ)⟩=⟨1H,χ⁡(ResH​(ρ))⟩H,\langle\text{Ind}^{G}_{H}(1_{H}),\chi(\rho)\rangle=\langle 1_{H},\chi(\text{Res}_{H}(\rho))\rangle_{H},

where χ⁡(ρ)\chi(\rho) is the character of the irrep χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\irr(G) given by its traces, and ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle is the inner product between class functions.

The left-hand side ⟨IndHG​(1H),χ⁡(ρ)⟩\langle\text{Ind}^{G}_{H}(1_{H}),\chi(\rho)\rangle is nonzero if and only if ρ\rho is an irreducible component of the permutation representation of GG on G/HG/H. The right-hand side ⟨1H,χ⁡(ResH​(ρ))⟩H\langle 1_{H},\chi(\text{Res}_{H}(\rho))\rangle_{H} is nonzero if and only if dim​(VH)≠0\text{dim}(V^{H})\neq 0

∎

Note that this lemma also works for 1g​H1_{gH} for a coset g​HgH, since Fourier transforms turns the translation action by gg into group multiplication by ρ⁡(g)\rho(g).

In the double coset circuit, we are specifically interested in the membership counting functions. More specifically, let H1,⋯,HnH_{1},\cdots,H_{n} be a collection of conjugate subgroups of GG. Given an element σ∈G\sigma\in G, define the membership counting function as

F⁡(σ)=∑i=1n1σ​Hi.F(\sigma)=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}1_{\sigma H_{i}}.

Combining all previous results, we have the following corollary describing the membership counting function FF.

Corollary G.5.

If the permutation representation of GG on G/H1G/H_{1} has only 22 irreducible components, the Fourier transform F^\hat{F} of the membership counting function FF is nonzero only at these 22 irreducible components. In particular, the equation (11) applies to FF.

One may wonder how restrictive it is for the permutation representation on G/HG/H to only have 22 irreducible components. The follow lemma shows that it applies to our case when G=SnG=S_{n} and H=Sn−1H=S_{n-1}.

Lemma G.6.

For SnS_{n} and the subgroup Sn−1S_{n-1} fixing one element, the permutation representation has only two irreducible components.

Proof.

The natural representation of SnS_{n} on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} (by permuting the basis) decomposes as a direct sum of trivial representation and the standard representation of dimension n−1n-1. ∎

Indeed, we see that when looking at the action of an individual neuron on the prediction space (i.e. “if this neuron fires, which predictions become more likely and which less?”), we see that it is only neurons that are predicting the same coset that are correlated. The average pairwise correlation of neuron actions is uncorrelated, as is the correlation of neurons associated with the same irrep. Refer to Table 3 for the full results.

G.3 An Asymptotic Analysis

Our theory of coset circuits and the GCR algorithm of [Chughtai et al. 2023] cannot be equivalent because there is no one-to-one relationship between irreps and subgroups. Even for S5S_{5}, there are more subgroups than irreps. Quantitatively speaking, the irreps already fail to catch up with the number of subgroups. For the direct comparison of SnS_{n} refer to

Asymptotically, the number of subgroups of SnS_{n} is bounded below as follows (see Pyber 1993):

2(116+o⁡(1))​n2≤|Sub​(Sn)|,2^{(\frac{1}{16}+o(1))n^{2}}\leq|\text{Sub}(S_{n})|,

whereas the number of irreps of SnS_{n} is asymptotically the following (see Erdos 1942):

|Irr⁡(Sn)|∼14​n⋅312​eπ​(23)12​n12.|\irr(S_{n})|\sim\dfrac{1}{4n\cdot 3^{\frac{1}{2}}}e^{\pi(\frac{2}{3})^{\frac{1}{2}}n^{\frac{1}{2}}}.

We see that the former has a much higher asymptotic growth than the latter.

In practice, as can be seen in Table 5, many subgroups concentrate on more than one irrep. We do not have an explanation for why the coset circuits always do concentrate one irrep. In practice, the different values for the cosets are arranged so that the contributions of all but one irrep cancel out. We hypothesize that it may have something to do with the margin maximization effect discussed in [Morwani et al. 2024]. As we mention in the main body, we observe that subgroups which concentrate on more than one irrep will form coset circuits that concentrate entirely on any of the irreps, while still behaving equivalently. We do not think that there is in fact a connection between what the circuit is doing the irrep.

For a subgroup H≤GH\leq G, we can investigate the Fourier transform of the indicator function 1H1_{H} by looking at its evaluation at each irrep. Concretely, we first center the indicator function by defining

f⁡(g)={−|H||G|,g∉H1−|H||G|,g∈H.f(g)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{|H|}{|G|},~g\not\in H\\ 1-\dfrac{|H|}{|G|},~g\in H.\end{cases}

By doing so, f^\hat{f} evaluates to 00 on the trivial representation of GG.

Given an irrep ρ∈Irr⁡(G)\rho\in\irr(G), we first denote the value of the Fourier transform of ff at ρ\rho by f^|ρ\hat{f}|_{\rho}. The contribution of ρ\rho to f^\hat{f} is defined by the following:

‖f^|ρ‖2∑δ∈Irr⁡(G)‖f^|δ‖2\dfrac{\|\hat{f}|_{\rho}\|^{2}}{\sum\limits_{\delta\in\irr(G)}\|\hat{f}|_{\delta}\|^{2}}

Here, we list all the conjugacy classes of subgroups of S5S_{5} and how each irrep of S5S_{5} contributes to their centered indicator function. We center the indicator function to remove the contribution of the trivial irrep, which is only based on the index of the subgroup. This step makes the contributions comparable. In the first column, we show the homomorphism type of each subgroup. Recall that two groups G,G′G,G^{\prime} are homomorphic if there exists a function f:G→G′f:G\rightarrow G^{\prime} such that for all g,h∈Gg,\;h\in G, f⁡(g​h)=f⁡(g)​f​(h)f(gh)=f(g)f(h). Every group within a conjugacy class is a homomorphic, with the homomorphism of two subgroups H,H′H,\;H^{\prime} of GG given by conjugation by an element of g∈Gg\in G, h↦g​h​g−1h\mapsto ghg^{-1}. Two conjugacy classes of subgroups, however, may be homomorphic as groups, but no homomorphism can be given as conjugation by an element of GG.
